1.title: Articles & Wanting
1.context: French nouns are either masculine (le) or feminine (la). Every -ion word is feminine without exception. Object pronouns le and la go before the verb.
1.grammar: The -ion ending is 100% reliable: every French noun ending in -ion is feminine. When a noun starts with a vowel, le and la both shorten to l'. Object pronouns (le = it/him, la = it/her) always go before the verb: Je le veux = I it want.

build: Pick the noun gender first: le for masculine, la for feminine.
Before a vowel, compress le/la to l'.
If the English says it, move le/la before veux.
writing: Apostrophes matter in l’opinion and l’organisation.
Final x in veux is written but silent.
Accent marks in café and gâteau must be typed.
traps: Do not put it after the verb as in English.
Do not guess gender for -ion words in this track; treat them as feminine.

2.title: -ation → -er Rule
2.context: Almost every English -ation word has a French -ation counterpart. Remove -ation and add -er to get the French verb. Un peu means a little.
2.grammar: The rule works because Latin -ationem nouns directly correspond to -are verbs. French simplified both to -ation and -er. Test: does the English word have a clear verb? Célébration → célébrer works. Nation doesn't (no verb *natier). Un peu = a little — two words in French.
sentences: Do you want to visit a little?
I want to explore the tradition.
Do you want to transform something?
I want to celebrate the collection.
Do you want to participate a little?
I want to illustrate the organisation.

build: Find the English -ation idea, then form the French -ation noun or -er verb.
After veux, keep the next verb in the infinitive.
If a pronoun belongs to the infinitive, place it before that infinitive.
writing: Many -ation nouns look English-like but keep French accents elsewhere.
French infinitives here end in -er.
Write un peu as two words.
traps: Do not translate to as a separate word before -er infinitives.
Do not move object pronouns after the infinitive.

3.title: Modal Verbs
3.context: Je peux (I can) works exactly like je veux — both are modal verbs followed by an infinitive. Quelque chose means something. Recommander and commander share the mander root.
3.grammar: Modals (vouloir, pouvoir) are always followed by an infinitive — the to-form. In French the 'to' is built into the infinitive ending -er, so no separate word needed: je peux réserver = I can reserve. The COM-/CON- prefix means 'together/with': com-mander, con-firmer, com-pliquer.
sentences: Je veux, mais je ne peux pas.
I want to, but I can't.
Je peux commander quelque chose plus tard.

build: Choose veux or peux as the first verb.
Leave the action verb in the infinitive.
Use quelque chose when the English says something.
writing: Peux keeps final x silent but written.
Quelque chose is two words.
Watch double m in recommander and commander.
traps: Do not conjugate the second verb after peux.
Do not split quelque chose with an article.

4.title: Inversion Questions
4.context: Peux-tu and veux-tu are inverted question forms — more formal than rising intonation. The dash links verb and subject. Fermer means to close.
4.grammar: French has three question strategies: (1) intonation only: Tu veux ? (2) est-ce que (Track 22): Est-ce que tu veux ? (3) inversion: Veux-tu ? Special case: inverting je with peux gives the archaic puis-je, preserved only for this construction.
words: can I? (archaic inversion of je peux)
sentences: Do you want to explore something?
Veux-tu fermer la porte un peu ?
Do you want to close the door a little?
Do you want to celebrate the tradition?
Peux-tu fermer la porte plus tard ?
Can you close the door later?

build: For formal questions, invert verb and subject.
Link the inverted verb and pronoun with a hyphen.
Keep the action verb in the infinitive after peux or veux.
writing: Hyphens are part of inversion: peux-tu, veux-tu.
Puis-je is the special inversion of je peux.
Final r in fermer is written in the infinitive.
traps: Do not write peux tu without a hyphen in inversion practice.
Do not use peux-je; the preserved form is puis-je.

5.title: De, Plus Tard, Clé
5.context: De means of/from and shows possession. Plus tard means later. Fermer à clé means to lock (close with a key). The PLIC/PLEX family comes from Latin plicare = to fold.
5.grammar: De is the most versatile preposition — it shows possession: les clés de la voiture = the car keys. Plus means 'more' in comparatives (plus tard = later) and 'not anymore' in negation (ne…plus, Track 35). Expliquer = ex+plier = to unfold. Compliquer = com+plier = to fold together.
words: with a key → fermer à clé = to lock
sentences: Je veux fermer la porte à clé plus tard.
I want to lock the door later.
Do you want a bit of cake?
Peux-tu organiser quelque chose plus tard ?
Je veux réserver quelque chose un peu plus tard.
I want to reserve something a little later.
Je veux un peu de café.
I want a bit of coffee.

build: Use de to connect possession or amount.
Use plus tard for later.
For a little of something, build un peu de + noun.
writing: À clé needs the accent on à and é in clé.
Plus tard is two words.
Explain-family verbs often keep -quer spelling.
traps: Do not use English apostrophe-S possession.
Do not drop de after un peu when a noun follows.

6.title: Je Dois
6.context: Je dois means both I must and I owe — obligation as debt. Tu dois works the same. La voiture is the car. The OI combination always sounds like /wha/.
6.grammar: Je dois (I must/I owe) — the debt metaphor for obligation is in both French and English: 'I owe it to them to fix this.' The OI combination reliably gives the /wha/ sound: dois, voir, voiture, moi, toi. Final silent-E activates the preceding consonant: la voiture (R pronounced), le port (T silent).
sentences: Peux-tu réparer la voiture plus tard ?
Can you repair the car later?

build: Use dois for must or owe.
Put the action after dois in the infinitive.
Use de for car-key style possession.
writing: Oi in dois, voiture, moi, toi sounds like /wa/.
Final s in dois is written but silent.
Réparer and préparer differ by prefix.
traps: Do not add a separate to before French infinitives.
Do not pronounce written final consonants just because you type them.

7.title: Maintenant & the Train
7.context: Maintenant means now. Le train and le bus are the transport options. À temps means on time. The accent grave (è) signals the open /eh/ sound.
7.grammar: Maintenant literally means 'maintaining in the present' — from maintenir + now. Accents signal pronunciation: accent grave (è) = open /eh/ sound as in réserver, réparer. Without accent, E gives the muffled /uh/ sound. The nasal rule: N or M at the end of a syllable gets swallowed into the vowel.
sentences: Can you confirm the visit now?
I want to reserve the train.
Tu dois confirmer la visite plus tard.
You must confirm the visit later.
Peux-tu recommander le train ou le bus ?
Can you recommend the train or the bus?
Je veux prendre le train maintenant.
I want to take the train now.

build: Use maintenant for now and à temps for on time.
Choose le train or le bus as transport nouns.
Keep modal + infinitive structure when combining with earlier tracks.
writing: À temps needs accent on à.
Maintenant has a nasal vowel and silent final t.
Accent grave marks open è in words like près later.
traps: Do not translate on time literally word by word.
Do not forget articles before train and bus.

8.title: Object Pronouns
8.context: Le (it/him) and la (it/her) go before the verb they belong to — not after like in English. With two verbs, the pronoun goes before the second verb (the action verb).
8.grammar: Object pronouns always go before the verb they belong to. With two verbs (want + to repair): the pronoun goes before the second: je veux le réparer = I want it to-repair. The l' contraction works for pronouns too: l'organiser = to organise it. The -ette ending (baguette, bicyclette) is always feminine — a diminutive that lost its 'small' meaning.
sentences: Je veux la préparer plus tard.
I want to prepare it later.
Can you confirm it on time?

build: Identify the thing: masculine le, feminine la, plural les.
With two verbs, place the pronoun before the action infinitive.
Before a vowel, use l'.
writing: Apostrophe in l’organiser is required.
Infinitive -er often sounds like é but is written -er.
Many -ette nouns are feminine.
traps: Do not place the pronoun before veux when it belongs to the second verb.
Do not write le organiser before a vowel.

9.title: Voir & Me/Te
9.context: Voir (to see) is an -IR verb. Me means me and te means you as object pronouns — they follow the same position rules as le/la. Invoquer, provoquer share the voquer root.
9.grammar: Voir ends in -IR — the second conjugation. The voquer root (Latin vocare = to call) appears in: pro-voquer (call forth), in-voquer (call in), é-voquer (evoke), con-voquer (summon). Me and te follow identical rules to le/la — before the verb, contract before vowels: m'inviter (to invite me).
words: the party (fête = feast, circumflex hides S)
sentences: Je veux juste le voir plus tard.
I just want to see him later.
Do you want to see me?
I want to organise the party.
Je veux t'inviter à la fête.
I want to invite you to the party.
Elle veut m'inviter, mais je veux l'inviter.
She wants to invite me, but I want to invite her.

build: Use voir for to see.
Use me or te before the verb they belong to.
Contract me/te before a vowel: m’ or t’.
writing: Voir has oi spelling but /wa/ sound.
Apostrophes in m’inviter and t’inviter are not optional.
Fête has a circumflex.
traps: Do not confuse tu as subject with te as object.
Do not leave me/te after the verb.

10.title: Un/Une & Noir
10.context: Un is the masculine a/one, une is the feminine. Adjectives come after the noun in French. Présenter means to introduce/present. Noir/noire means black.
10.grammar: Un/une — gendered 'a' matching the noun. The E on une is the feminine marker, same E that appears on all feminine nouns. Adjectives follow the noun in French: le café noir (the coffee black). Final consonant of adjective becomes audible in the feminine: noir (silent R) → noire (R audible). Liaison: N in un resurfaces before vowels — un ami sounds like 'u-na-mi'.
sentences: Do you want a black coffee?
I want to prepare an invitation.
Tu dois préparer un café noir.
You must prepare a black coffee.
I want to invite a friend.
Do you want a black bicycle?

build: Choose un or une from the noun gender.
Put ordinary color adjectives after the noun.
Make adjectives agree when the noun is feminine.
writing: Une has final e; un does not.
Noire writes final e and pronounces the r.
Un ami can link in speech but stays two words.
traps: Do not put noir before café in these exercises.
Do not choose un/une based on the owner or speaker.

11.title: Il/Elle Doit
11.context: Il (he) and elle (she) use doit, veut, peut — forms with a silent T. The -ary → -aire pattern converts English adjectives directly. La fête d'anniversaire = birthday party.
11.grammar: Il/elle forms end in a silent T — the third-person marker from Latin. It surfaces in liaison: il doit_aller. The -ary → -aire pattern is very productive: ordinaire, documentaire, littéraire, populaire, solaire. The word volontaire (voluntary) shares the same Latin root as vouloir — both from volo = I want.
sentences: Elle veut m'inviter à la fête d'anniversaire.
She wants to invite me to the birthday party.
Il veut me voir, mais elle veut t'inviter.
He wants to see me, but she wants to invite you.
Elle doit organiser la fête, mais elle ne peut pas le faire maintenant.
She must organise the party, but she can't do it now.
Il veut le voir. Elle le veut aussi.
He wants to see it. She wants it too.

build: Switch je/tu forms to il or elle forms.
Use doit, veut, peut for he/she.
Let -ary English adjectives suggest French -aire.
writing: Third-person t in doit/veut/peut is written but usually silent.
Anniversaire has double n and double s.
Volontaire ends in -aire.
traps: Do not add an extra ending after il/elle forms.
Do not treat c’est and il est as interchangeable later.

12.title: Se Préparer & Portable
12.context: Se préparer = to get ready (prepare oneself). Reflexive verbs use se/me/te — a self pronoun. Le portable = the mobile phone (carriable device).
12.grammar: Reflexive verbs loop back to the subject: je me prépare (I prepare myself), tu te prépares, il se prépare. French uses reflexives for many actions English treats as simple intransitive: get ready, get up, get dressed, relax. Tu vs. te: tu = subject (acting), te = object (receiving). Exactly like English he/him, she/her.
sentences: Elle veut se relaxer un peu.
She wants to relax a little.
Il doit se préparer, mais il veut se relaxer d'abord.
He must get ready, but he wants to relax first.
Je veux t'inviter à la fête.
I want to invite you to the party.
Il doit se préparer plus tard.
Je dois te préparer et me préparer.
I must prepare you and get ready myself.

build: For actions done to oneself, add the reflexive pronoun.
Match the reflexive pronoun to the subject.
With a modal, place se before the infinitive.
writing: Se préparer has accent on é.
Je me, tu te, il se stay separate before consonants.
Portable is masculine in this course.
traps: Do not translate get ready without the self-pronoun.
Do not confuse te object with tu subject.

13.title: -able & Porter
13.context: The -able suffix means capable of being verbed. Porter means to carry/wear — one of French's most productive verbs. La barbe = the beard.
13.grammar: -able (from Latin -abilis) = capable of being [verbed]: port-able, ador-able, sépar-able. Work backwards: strip -able, add -er. Porter (to carry) family: apporter (bring = carry towards), emporter (take away = carry away), rapporter (bring back), supporter (tolerate — ⚠ not 'support'). Le portefeuille = wallet = carries-papers.
sentences: Je veux porter un pantalon noir.
I want to wear black trousers.
I want to grow a beard.
He wants to take the car away.
I want to bring something back.
She wants to carry the baguette.
Il doit rapporter la voiture et la réparer.
He must bring the car back and repair it.
Peux-tu apporter le café et le gâteau ?
Can you bring the coffee and the cake?

build: Use -able to mean capable of being done.
Use porter as carry/wear, then add prefixes for bring/take.
Keep support/tolerate meaning clear for supporter.
writing: -able looks familiar but still follows French spelling.
Portefeuille is one compound word.
Double consonants can appear in supporter.
traps: Do not assume supporter means to support/help.
Do not memorize every prefixed porter verb separately; build from the direction.

14.title: -ité & False Friends
14.context: The -ity → -ité pattern converts English -ity nouns directly. All -ité words are feminine. Supporter = to tolerate, not support. Bien means well (adverb).
14.grammar: -ité (from Latin -itas) = -ity in English. All -ité words are feminine. The É tells you the T is pronounced: la liberté, la qualité, la réalité, la capacité. False friends: supporter = to bear/tolerate; attendre = to wait (not attend); assister à = to attend. Bien = well (adverb); bon/bonne = good (adjective).
sentences: Il doit saisir la possibilité, mais il ne peut pas la supporter.
He must seize the possibility, but he can't tolerate her.
Je dois bien me comporter et saisir l'opportunité.
I must behave well and seize the opportunity.

build: Map English -ity to French -ité where useful.
Pause on false friends and check the actual meaning.
Use earlier article and adjective agreement rules.
writing: -ité usually carries acute é.
Opportunité is feminine.
French accents distinguish words that look English-like.
traps: Do not trust every English-looking word.
Do not drop gender just because the noun is abstract.

15.title: Tout le Monde & Mon/Ton
15.context: Tout le monde = everybody, takes he/she verb form. Mon/ton for masculine nouns, ma/ta for feminine — but mon/ton before any vowel regardless of gender.
15.grammar: Tout le monde veut — 'everybody' takes the he/she form, like English 'everybody wants'. Mon/ma, ton/ta: gender depends on the THING possessed, not the owner. Before vowels, always use mon/ton (not ma/ta): mon amie even though amie is feminine. Liaison: N resurfaces before vowels — mon_ami sounds like mo-na-mi.
sentences: My friend wants to invite you.
Tout le monde doit se préparer.
Tout le monde veut célébrer, mais mon ami ne peut pas venir.
Everybody wants to celebrate, but my friend can't come.
Mon ami veut m'inviter, mais ton ami veut t'inviter.
My friend wants to invite me, but your friend wants to invite you.
Tout le monde doit saisir l'opportunité.

build: Treat tout le monde like he/she for the verb.
Choose mon/ma/ton/ta from the possessed noun.
Before a vowel, use mon or ton even for feminine nouns.
writing: Tout le monde is three words.
Mon ami links in speech but remains two words.
Bien is written with -ien.
traps: Do not use plural verb after everybody.
Do not choose ma amie before a vowel.

16.title: Les & Attendre
16.context: Les = them (plural object pronoun). Attendre = to wait (RE verb). Finir = to finish (IR verb). Puis-je = the archaic can I, preserved only for inversion.
16.grammar: Les (them / the-plural): the E sounds different from le (/leh/ vs /luh/). Silent S becomes audible in liaison: les_inviter. RE verbs (attendre, perdre, vendre): remove -RE to get the present stem. The course now has all three verb families: -ER (most verbs), -IR (finir, voir), -RE (attendre). Puis-je is a linguistic fossil — the archaic form of peux-je preserved only for this inversion.
sentences: I want to wait for them.
Tout le monde veut le finir.
Je dois les voir et les inviter.
I must see them and invite them.
Puis-je attendre ton ami ? Il doit les voir.
Can I wait for your friend? He must see them.

build: Use les for plural the or them.
Use attendre for to wait for.
Place object les before the verb it belongs to.
writing: Plural s is often written but silent.
Les can mean the or them depending on position.
Attendre has double t.
traps: Do not add pour after attendre for wait for.
Do not confuse les article with les object; position tells you.

17.title: New ER Verbs & Plurals
17.context: All new verbs entering French become -ER verbs — googler, zapper, tweeter. Plural nouns add silent -S. Les signals plurality, not the noun's sound.
17.grammar: -ER is the only open verb class in French — all neologisms join it: googler, zapper, streamer, tweeter. Plural nouns add -S but it's silent. You hear plurality from les (/leh/), not from the noun. Exception: -AL → -AUX in plural (animal → animaux, journal → journaux). Liaison S sounds like Z between vowels: les_amis → /le-za-mi/.
sentences: Do you want to invite them?
Ils les veulent. Tu les veux aussi ?
They want them. Do you want them too?
Je veux les googler et les inviter.
I want to google them and invite them.

build: For je/il ER present, remove -er and use the stem sound.
Use known nouns and verbs to make new combinations.
Keep articles and pronouns doing the structure work.
writing: ER infinitive and é past forms will matter later.
Je forms can hide final written letters.
Plural nouns still need plural articles.
traps: Do not over-conjugate every verb form yet.
Do not drop articles in short noun phrases.

18.title: Au/Du & Aller
18.context: À + le = au, de + le = du. These contractions only happen with le. La, l', les never contract. Aller = to go. Le mari = the husband. Le bureau = the office.
18.grammar: Au (à+le) and du (de+le) contract only with masculine singular le. Full system: à+le=au, à+la=à la, à+les=aux, de+le=du, de+les=des. The -age ending is masculine (from Latin -aticum neuter): le village, le mariage, le message, le passage. Exception: la cage.
sentences: Je dois aller à la gare.
I must go to the station.
You must go to the office.
Elle veut aller à la maison.
I want to see my husband.
He wants to go to the village.
Mon mari veut aller au village, mais elle veut aller à la maison.
My husband wants to go to the village, but she wants to go home.
Je dois aller au garage pour réparer la voiture.
I must go to the garage to repair the car.
Elle veut aller à la gare à temps.
She wants to go to the station on time.

build: Contract à + le to au and de + le to du.
Use aller for to go.
Use à for destination and de for from/of.
writing: Au and du are one-word contractions.
Aller has irregular forms.
À keeps its accent when not contracted.
traps: Do not write à le or de le before masculine singular le.
Do not contract before la or l’.

19.title: Ne…Pas & Je Suis
19.context: Ne…pas is the two-part negation sandwich around the verb. Je suis = I am, from être (to be). Envoyer = to send. Montrer = to show.
19.grammar: Ne…pas: originally ne alone was negation (from Latin non). It weakened so speakers added pas (step) for emphasis. Now pas is standard; in spoken French ne is often dropped: je veux pas. Five negation patterns in this course: ne…pas, ne…rien (Track 23), ne…jamais (Track 34), ne…plus (Track 35), ne…que (Track 32). Je suis from Latin sum = same root as 'sum total'.
sentences: Je ne peux pas organiser quelque chose.
Je dois te montrer quelque chose.
Je ne veux pas te montrer ça.
I don't want to show you that.
Il ne doit pas fermer la porte.

build: Put ne before the conjugated verb and pas after it.
With two verbs, the negative surrounds the first verb.
Use je suis for I am.
writing: Ne becomes n' before a vowel.
Pas is separate and comes after the conjugated verb.
Suis keeps final s silent.
traps: Do not put pas at the end automatically.
Do not put ne before the infinitive in these modal patterns.

20.title: Ne Peux Pas & Trouver
20.context: Ne peux pas = can't. Trouver = to find (same root as treasure trove). Garer = to park (from gare). La maison = the house.
20.grammar: Vocabulary built from nouns: la gare (station) → garer (to park/station). La marche (walk) → marcher (to walk). Trouver and English 'trove' are the same word — Latin tropus (a figure of speech, an unexpected find). Clé vocabulary: les clés de la voiture = the car keys. French uses de + noun where English uses compound nouns or apostrophe-S.
sentences: Je ne peux pas garer la voiture.
Mon mari ne peut pas trouver les clés de la maison.
My husband can't find the house keys.
Je ne peux pas trouver les clés.
Tu dois trouver la clé de la voiture.
You must find the car key.
Il ne peut pas les trouver.
Je ne peux pas garer la voiture parce que je ne peux pas trouver la clé.
I can't park the car because I can't find the key.
Elle ne peut pas garer la voiture maintenant.
She can't park the car now.
Mon ami ne peut pas trouver la maison.
My friend can't find the house.

build: Build can’t as ne peux pas.
Place object pronouns before trouver when they are the thing found.
Use de for keys of the house/car.
writing: Peux keeps x written.
Clés has accent and plural s.
Maison is feminine: la maison.
traps: Do not forget both ne and pas.
Do not translate car keys with English word order.

21.title: Chercher & Notre/Ma/Ta
21.context: Chercher = to look for (no separate for needed). Notre = our (same for masc. and fem.). Ma/ta for feminine, mon/ton for masculine nouns.
21.grammar: Chercher incorporates 'for': je cherche la voiture = I look-for the car. Same with attendre: j'attends le train = I wait-for the train. Notre (our) doesn't have gender variants — unlike mon/ma, ton/ta. Same applies to votre (your, formal) and singular leur (their). Son/sa = his/her following the same pattern as mon/ma.
sentences: I must look for our car.
Can you look for my wife?
Je ne peux pas trouver ma voiture.
Je veux l'envoyer à mon ami.
I want to send it to my friend.
Elle ne peut pas trouver sa voiture.
Je ne peux pas trouver ma voiture. Peux-tu la chercher ?
I can't find my car. Can you look for it?
Il ne peut pas trouver son ami.

build: Use chercher for to look for/search.
Use trouver only when actually finding.
Choose possessives from the noun possessed.
writing: Notre does not change for gender in the same way mon/ma does.
Chercher keeps ch spelling.
Ma/ta become mon/ton before vowels.
traps: Do not use pour after chercher.
Do not confuse looking for with finding.

22.title: Essayer De & Où
22.context: Essayer de + infinitif = to try to do. Où = where. Est = is (silent EST). Tu es = you are. D'où = from where.
22.grammar: Essayer de uses de as a bridge to the infinitive. Other verbs needing de: décider de, arrêter de, refuser de. Verbs needing nothing: vouloir, pouvoir, devoir. Est (is) spelled EST but all consonants silent. You've now seen: suis (I am), es (you are), est (he/she/it is) — all from the irregular verb être.
words: I try to (de bridges to infinitive)
sentences: I'm trying to find the keys.
Où est la clé de la voiture ?
J'essaye de trouver ma voiture. Où est-elle ?
I'm trying to find my car. Where is it?
Elle n'est pas d'ici. Elle est d'où ?
She's not from here. Where is she from?
Tu es où ? J'essaye de te trouver.
Where are you? I'm trying to find you.

build: Use essayer de before an infinitive.
Use où for where.
Choose suis/es/est from the subject.
writing: Où needs accent; ou without accent means or.
D'ici contracts de + ici.
J'essaye uses apostrophe before vowel.
traps: Do not drop de after essayer.
Do not confuse où and ou in dictation.

23.title: ER Present & Ne…Rien
23.context: In sound, all four singular ER verb forms (I, you, he, she) are identical — the infinitive minus -ER. Ne…rien = not anything / nothing. Regretter = to regret.
23.grammar: ER present tense: all singular forms sound like the infinitive minus -ER: manger → mange for je/tu/il/elle. Differences exist in writing (je mange, tu manges, il mange) but none are audible. Ne…rien: rien is a pronoun (nothing/anything) that replaces the object. Unlike pas (a particle), rien goes where an object would go.
sentences: Elle ne mange rien, et elle ne regrette rien.
She doesn't eat anything, and she doesn't regret anything.
Il mange, mais elle ne veut rien manger.
He eats, but she doesn't want to eat anything.
Je mange, je célèbre, je ne regrette rien.
I eat, I celebrate, I don't regret anything.
Elle ne veut pas manger. Il doit lui montrer quelque chose.
She doesn't want to eat. He must show her something.

build: Use present ER stems for I/you/he/she.
Build nothing as ne...rien.
Keep object pronouns before the verb.
writing: Rien is separate after the verb.
Silent endings make several written forms sound alike.
Accents still matter in typed answers.
traps: Do not use pas and rien together in standard practice.
Do not assume identical sound means identical spelling.

24.title: Tu Form & Habiter
24.context: Tu form of ER verbs adds silent -ES. Habiter = to live somewhere, with silent H. Mais = but. Living near a place expressed with près de.
24.grammar: Tu form: ER verbs remove -ER and add -ES (silent): tu manges, tu fermes, tu habites. The S triggers liaison before vowels: tu manges_et bois (S becomes Z). Habiter: the H is mute (from Latin), triggering contraction: j'habite. Two H types in French: mute H (from Latin — triggers elision) and aspirate H (from Germanic — doesn't).
words: the habit (same root — what you live with)
sentences: Je ne suis pas d'ici mais j'habite ici.
I'm not from here but I live here.
Elle habite près de la gare.
Il n'habite pas ici mais il mange ici tous les jours.
He doesn't live here but he eats here every day.
Tu habites ici ? Tu manges où ?
Do you live here? Where do you eat?
Elle habite près de l'école mais elle n'étudie pas là.
She lives near the school but she doesn't study there.

build: For tu ER verbs, write final -s even when silent.
Use habiter for to live.
Combine location phrases from earlier tracks.
writing: Tu forms often have silent final s.
J'habite contracts before h in writing here.
Près has accent grave.
traps: Do not omit the written tu-form s.
Do not over-pronounce final s just because you type it.

25.title: SP/ST→S & Arrêter
25.context: French dropped the S before hard consonants (SP, ST, SC). A circumflex often marks where an S was lost. Arrêter (de) = to stop (doing). Étudier = to study.
25.grammar: Latin schola → école; hospitale → hôpital; bestia → bête; festum → fête. The circumflex (^) was added to remember the missing S — it's a memorial to a lost consonant. Whenever you see a circumflex, look for the S in the English cognate: forêt/forest, côte/coast, pâte/paste, fête/feast. S'arrêter = to stop oneself; arrêter de + infinitive = to stop doing.
sentences: I live close to the school.
J'habite près de l'école mais j'étudie près de l'hôpital.
I live near the school but I study near the hospital.
J'arrête de fumer parce que j'étudie près de l'hôpital.
I'm quitting smoking because I study near the hospital.

build: Use arrêter de for stop doing.
Use s’arrêter for stop oneself/come to a stop.
Notice old S patterns in école/hôpital/forêt.
writing: Circumflex often marks a lost s: forêt/forest.
Arrêter has double r and accent.
S'arrêter needs apostrophe before vowel.
traps: Do not use arrêter de and s’arrêter the same way.
Do not forget de before an infinitive after arrêter.

26.title: Que/Pourquoi & Je Sais
26.context: Que serves as what (in questions), that (conjunction), and more. Je sais = I know. Venir = to come (irregular IR verb). Pourquoi = for what = why.
26.grammar: Que has five jobs: (1) what in questions: que manges-tu ? (2) that as conjunction: je sais que… (3) part of qu'est-ce que (4) than in comparisons: plus grand que (Track 32) (5) only in ne…que (Track 32). VEN- root (from Latin venire): souvenir (memory = comes back), avenue (comes towards), bienvenu (welcome = well-come), devenir (become), revenir (come back).
sentences: Je sais que tu veux venir.
I know that you want to come.
Pourquoi tu ne veux pas manger ?
Why don't you want to eat?
Je sais ce qu'elle veut, mais elle ne parle que le français.
I know what she wants, but she only speaks French.
Elle veut revenir. Tu sais pourquoi ?
She wants to come back. Do you know why?
Je sais qu'elle doit venir et inviter tout le monde.
I know that she must come and invite everybody.
Pourquoi il ne veut pas venir ? Je ne sais pas.
Why doesn't he want to come? I don't know.

build: Use que for that in I know that...
Use pourquoi for why.
Use sais/sait forms for knowing a fact.
writing: Pourquoi is one word.
Je sais ends with silent s.
Qu'il/Qu'elle contracts que before a vowel.
traps: Do not use ce que when you only mean that.
Do not translate why as pour quoi in normal questions.

27.title: Parler & F→P Shift
27.context: Parler = to speak, a regular ER verb. The F→P shift: English kept Germanic F where French kept Latin P. À pied = on foot. De quoi = about what.
27.grammar: The F→P shift happened when Norman French and Anglo-Saxon met after 1066. English kept the Germanic F, French kept the Latin P: foot/pied, father/père, fish/poisson, few/peu, for/pour, feather/plume. De quoi parles-tu ? — the preposition de stays with its verb even when the question word moves to the front. This is the same in English: 'what are you talking about?' keeps 'about' at the end.
words: to speak about (de stays with verb)
sentences: Notre père ne parle pas le français.
Je ne veux pas aller à la maison à pied.
I don't want to go home on foot.
Elle parle à mon père. Pourquoi ? Je ne sais pas.
She speaks to my father. Why? I don't know.
Il ne parle pas le français. Il est d'où ?
He doesn't speak French. Where is he from?
Je parle un peu français. De quoi parles-tu ?
I speak a little French. What are you talking about?
Notre père va à pied. Il ne parle pas le français.
Our father goes on foot. He doesn't speak French.

build: Use parler à for speaking to someone.
Use parler de for speaking about something.
Use lui/leur later for to him/her/them.
writing: Parler is an ER infinitive.
Français has ç and accent.
À marks to in parler à.
traps: Do not make parler take a direct object for people.
Do not confuse French the language with French nationality adjectives.

28.title: Au/Du Full & Perdre
28.context: The full contraction system: au, du, aux, des. Ils/elles = they. Perdre = to lose (RE verb). Pêcher = to fish. Le poisson = the fish.
28.grammar: Full contraction system: à+le=au, à+les=aux, de+le=du, de+les=des (of the = some). La, l' never contract. Ils/elles: il and ils sound the same (/il/); distinction only in writing and liaison — ils_ont (the S becomes audible). Perdre = lose; the -DRE ending feels heavier than -ER verbs — the consonant cluster is more audible.
sentences: Tu dois goûter le poisson du village.
You must try the fish from the village.
Notre père ne veut pas aller au village.
Our father doesn't want to go to the village.
Ils doivent aller à la gare.
They must go to the station.
Je ne veux pas perdre les clés.
I don't want to lose the keys.
Ils veulent aller au village pour pêcher. Elle ne peut pas y aller à pied.
They want to go to the village to fish. She can't go on foot.
They want to go to the office.
Notre père veut goûter le poisson du village.
Our father wants to taste the fish from the village.

build: Use perdre for to lose.
Use au/du contractions before masculine le.
Use RE verb logic as a new family.
writing: Perdre keeps d in spelling though often silent in forms.
Au/du are one word.
Apartment/appartement has double p.
traps: Do not write de le after losing something from the office.
Do not treat RE verbs exactly like ER verbs.

29.title: Ils Veulent & Pour
29.context: Ils veulent (they want) keeps the L from the vol- root. Pour + infinitif = in order to. Payer = to pay. The V in doivent/peuvent/veulent is a Latin vestige.
29.grammar: Ils veulent: the L comes from Latin vol- (to want/will) — same as 'volunteer, volition'. Je veux is actually more contracted than ils veulent. Notice the V in ils peuvent, ils veulent, ils doivent — a vestige of Latin endings for these verb types. Pour + infinitif = in order to. Test: if you can say 'in order to' in English, use pour in French.
sentences: Ils doivent attendre ici pour payer.
They must wait here to pay.
They don't want to lose anything.
Je dois aller à la ville pour trouver les clés du garage.
I must go to town to find the garage keys.
Ils veulent venir, mais ils ne savent pas pourquoi.
They want to come, but they don't know why.
Pourquoi ils veulent attendre ici ? Ils doivent payer d'abord.
Why do they want to wait here? They must pay first.
Je dois aller au bureau pour payer et organiser quelque chose.
I must go to the office to pay and organise something.

build: Use ils forms for they.
Use pour + infinitive for in order to.
Keep modal + infinitive structure from earlier tracks.
writing: Final -ent is silent in many they forms but written.
Veulent/peuvent/doivent have internal spelling changes.
Pour is separate before the infinitive.
traps: Do not pronounce -ent as English ent.
Do not use pour when English to is just an infinitive after a modal.

30.title: ENT Silent & S'Appeler
30.context: The -ent ending on verbs (ils mangent) is completely silent. S'appeler = to be called (one calls oneself). Comment = how. Oublier = to forget (same root as oblivion).
30.grammar: Silent ENT: the third-person plural verb ending is never pronounced. French effectively made the 'they' verb ending inaudible, relying on the pronoun and context. Before vowels, the consonant before ENT can surface via liaison: ils mangent_et. Oublier and oblivion share Latin oblivisci. Comment = 'in what manner' — same word as English 'comment' but meaning split: French kept 'how', English took the noun.
sentences: They fish in order to eat.
I want to find an apartment.
Ils oublient toujours. Comment tu t'appelles encore ?
They always forget. What's your name again?
Il oublie tout mais n'oublie jamais de manger.
He forgets everything but never forgets to eat.
Elle oublie de payer. Il ne sait pas pourquoi.
She forgets to pay. He doesn't know why.

build: Use ils/elles + silent -ent for they verbs.
Use s’appeler for to be called.
Use comment for how/what in name questions.
writing: Third-person plural -ent is written but silent.
S'appeler uses apostrophe.
Oublier is linked to oblivion and keeps ou spelling.
traps: Do not pronounce -ent.
Do not translate what is your name word-for-word.

31.title: Faire & Qu'est-ce Que
31.context: Faire = to do/make (irregular RE verb). Qu'est-ce que = what (frozen expression, no inversion needed after it). Acheter = to buy (vowel alternation in stem).
31.grammar: Faire connects to English via Latin facere: fait (fact = something done), parfait (perfect = par+fait = thoroughly done), satisfaire (to satisfy = do enough). Qu'est-ce que is a frozen expression meaning 'what' — it already contains the question, so no inversion needed after it: qu'est-ce que tu veux ? Acheter: vowel strengthens when stressed — j'achète (strong E) vs. acheter (weak E).
sentences: What do you want to do?
Je ne peux pas le faire.
What do they want to eat?
Je sais que tu veux l'acheter.
I know that you want to buy it.
Qu'est-ce qu'ils veulent faire ce soir ? Je ne sais pas.
What do they want to do tonight? I don't know.
Qu'est-ce que tu veux acheter ? Je peux essayer de le trouver.
What do you want to buy? I can try to find it for you.

build: Use faire for do/make.
Use qu'est-ce que for what questions.
Use acheter/achète vowel change in present forms.
writing: Qu'est-ce que has apostrophe and hyphens.
Achète takes accent grave in the stressed form.
Faire has irregular spelling.
traps: Do not invert again after qu’est-ce que.
Do not confuse faire with fabriquer for every make context.

32.title: Ce Que & Parce Que
32.context: Ce que = what (the thing that) vs. que alone (that). Parce que = because. Ne…que = only. Partir = to leave/depart. Bientôt = soon.
32.grammar: Ce que vs. que: je sais que tu veux (I know THAT you want) vs. je sais ce que tu veux (I know WHAT you want = the thing that you want). Parce que = par + ce + que = 'by way of the thing that' = because. Ne…que (only): bookends around the verb — ne before, que before the restricted element: il ne parle que le français = he speaks only French.
sentences: Je sais ce que tu veux.
Il ne parle que le français.
Je ne peux pas manger parce que je dois partir.
I can't eat because I must leave.
Tu sais ce que tu dois faire ?
Do you know what you have to do?
Je sais ce qu'elle veut, mais elle ne parle que le français.
I know what she wants, but she only speaks French.
Je dois partir bientôt parce que je ne sais pas ce qu'elle veut.
I must leave soon because I don't know what she wants.
Elle ne mange que du poisson. Tu sais pourquoi ?
She only eats fish. Do you know why?

build: Use ce que for what as the thing that.
Use parce que for because.
Use ne...que for only.
writing: Parce que is two words.
Ce que is two words.
Ne...que brackets the verb and the limited element.
traps: Do not use que alone when English means what.
Do not confuse ne...que with a normal negative.

33.title: C'est vs Il Est & Adverbs
33.context: C'est refers to a situation or unnamed thing. Il/elle est refers to a specific gendered noun. Adjectives agree in gender and number. -ément = -ly adverbs.
33.grammar: C'est vs. il/elle est: c'est parfait (situation), il est parfait (referring to a masc. noun). Adjective agreement: base = masculine singular. Feminine: add -E (grand → grande, D becomes audible). Plural: add -S. The -ément suffix (like English -ly) attaches to any adjective: général → généralement, total → totalement, parfait → parfaitement.
sentences: C'est parfait mais ce n'est pas légal. C'est le problème.
It's perfect but it's not legal. That's the problem.
Elle est parfaite. Il est arrogant. Ils sont différents.
She is perfect. He is arrogant. They are different.
Normalement c'est urgent mais aujourd'hui ce n'est pas important.
Normally it's urgent but today it's not important.

build: Use c’est for a situation or unnamed thing.
Use il/elle est for a specific noun.
Add agreement to adjectives and build -ément adverbs.
writing: C’est contracts ce + est.
Feminine adjective e can reveal a final consonant.
-ément adverbs often carry accent.
traps: Do not use il est for every English it is.
Do not forget adjective agreement in writing.

34.title: RE Verbs I/Tu & Jamais
34.context: RE verbs (je/tu form): remove -RE, add -S. Je fais/tu fais, j'attends/tu attends. Ne…jamais = never. Ce soir = tonight.
34.grammar: RE verbs (je/tu): unlike ER verbs (just remove -ER), RE verbs remove -RE and add -S: attendre → j'attends, tu attends; faire → je fais, tu fais. Silent S. Note: j'attends and à temps (on time) sound identical — both have silent consonant clusters. Ne…jamais: from Latin jam magis = 'at any time'. Alone (without ne): si jamais tu veux = if you ever want.
sentences: Je ne fais rien ce soir.
Je ne fais jamais rien ce soir parce que j'attends toujours.
I never do anything tonight because I'm always waiting.
Tu ne le fais jamais et tu n'attends jamais. Qu'est-ce que tu fais ?
You never do it and you never wait. What do you do?
Je t'attends. Tu ne le fais jamais.
I'm waiting for you. You never do it.

build: For je/tu RE verbs, remove -re and add written -s.
Use ne...jamais for never.
Use attendre without an extra for.
writing: Je fais and tu fais look identical.
Attends has silent ds.
Jamais stays after the verb.
traps: Do not add pas with jamais in standard practice.
Do not omit written final s in je/tu RE forms.

35.title: Il Perd & Vendre
35.context: RE verb he/she form: no ending added — the final consonant is just silent. Il perd, il vend, il attend. ENT for 'they' makes the preceding consonant audible. Tout le temps = all the time.
35.grammar: RE verb he/she: no ending at all — il perd, il vend, il attend. The D is silent. This means I, he, she all sound identical for RE verbs. But ENT (they form) makes it audible: ils perdent (D audible) vs. il perd (D silent). Tout le temps = all the time. Toujours = always (tout + jour = all days). Le temps = both time and weather.
words: he loses (RE: no ending, D silent)
sentences: Tu les perds tout le temps.
You lose them all the time.
Il perd tout le temps mais il ne vend jamais. C'est étrange.
He loses all the time but he never sells. Strange.
Elle perd toujours mais tout le monde veut encore jouer.
She always loses but everybody still wants to play.
Il vend son appartement près de l'école.
He's selling his apartment near the school.

build: For il/elle RE verbs, use the stem with no added ending.
Use vend/perd/attend for he/she.
Use tout le temps for all the time.
writing: Il vend and il perd keep final d written but silent.
Ils vendent makes the d audible before silent -ent.
Toujours is one word.
traps: Do not add a written s to il/elle RE forms.
Do not pronounce final d in singular forms.

36.title: Nous/-Ons & Se Demander
36.context: Nous/-ons is the first verb ending with its own new sound (/oh/). Je me demande = I wonder (ask oneself). Si = if. Comprendre = com+prendre = to grasp together.
36.grammar: Nous + -ons: the first ending that actually adds a new sound. All other singular forms sound like the stem — but -ons adds /oh/: nous mangeons, nous vendons, nous perdons. Se demander = wonder (ask oneself). Comprendre = com + prendre (to take together = to grasp). Same root: apprendre (learn = take toward), surprendre (surprise = take from above), entreprendre (undertake = take between).
sentences: Je me demande si elle veut venir.
I wonder if she wants to come.
Nous nous demandons si tu veux le vendre.
We wonder if you want to sell it.
Nous comprenons, mais nous nous demandons pourquoi.
We understand, but we wonder why.
Je me demande si nous pouvons le faire. Nous devons partir bientôt.
I wonder if we can do it. We must leave soon.
Nous perdons toujours. Je me demande pourquoi.
We always lose. I wonder why.

build: Use nous + -ons for we.
Use se demander for wonder.
Use si to introduce if clauses.
writing: Nous forms add audible/written -ons.
Nous nous can appear in reflexive forms.
Comprendre keeps prendre spelling.
traps: Do not avoid nous nous when the verb is reflexive.
Do not use oui for if; use si in these clauses.

37.title: Lui/Leur & Cuisiner
37.context: Lui = to him/her (indirect object). Leur = to them (indirect). Direct objects: le/la/les. Test: can you put 'to' in front in English? If yes, use lui/leur.
37.grammar: Direct vs. indirect objects: direct (le/la/les) = thing acted on directly. Indirect (lui/leur) = who the action is directed toward. Test: 'I see him' → can't say 'I see to him' → direct → le. 'I speak to him' → indirect → lui. Nous serves all three roles: subject (we), object (us), indirect (to us). La cuisinière = the female cook AND the stove.
sentences: Je veux lui envoyer un message.
I want to send her a message.
Je veux leur envoyer un message.
I want to send them a message.
Nous pouvons leur cuisiner quelque chose.
I want to speak to him/her.
Elle lui parle mais il lui parle. Ils se parlent.
She speaks to him but he speaks to her. They speak to each other.
Nous pouvons leur cuisiner quelque chose, mais est-ce qu'ils veulent le manger ?
We can cook them something, but do they want to eat it?
Je veux leur envoyer un message et leur cuisiner quelque chose.
I want to send them a message and cook them something.

build: Ask whether English can use to before the person.
Use lui/leur for to him/her/them.
Keep le/la/les for direct objects.
writing: Lui and leur do not show gender.
Leur as pronoun has no s.
Cuisiner has cuisine spelling.
traps: Do not use le/la after verbs that mean to someone.
Do not add an s to leur when it is the pronoun.

38.title: Je Vais Future
38.context: Je vais + infinitif = I'm going to (going-to future). Aller's singular forms (vais/vas/va) come from Latin vadere — a different verb that merged with ambulare. Day names follow Latin planets.
38.grammar: Going-to future: identical to English in structure — je vais manger = I'm going to eat. Aller is irregular because two Latin verbs merged: vais/vas/va from vadere (to go urgently); allons/allez/vont from ambulare (to walk — same root as 'ambulance'). Day names: lundi (moon), mardi (Mars), mercredi (Mercury), jeudi (Jupiter), vendredi (Venus).
sentences: Are you going to buy it?
Je vais lui acheter quelque chose de bien.
I'm going to buy her something nice.
Elle va organiser la fête vendredi.
She's going to organise the party on Friday.
Je vais le faire demain. Je ne le fais pas ce soir.
I'm going to do it tomorrow. I'm not doing it tonight.
Il va perdre les clés. Elle va les trouver.
He's going to lose the keys. She's going to find them.
Nous allons leur montrer le village lundi.
We're going to show them the village on Monday.

build: Use aller + infinitive for going-to future.
Choose vais/vas/va/allons from the subject.
Keep the future action verb in the infinitive.
writing: Je vais has final s silent.
Days like lundi/vendredi are lowercase in French.
Demain is tomorrow.
traps: Do not conjugate the second verb after aller.
Do not treat going to a place and going to do as the same structure without checking the next word.

39.title: Passé Composé -é
39.context: The past tense most commonly used: avoir (to have) + past participle. ER verbs: remove -ER, add -É. J'ai mangé = I have eaten / I ate. Pas encore = not yet.
39.grammar: Passé composé: avoir + past participle. For ER verbs: remove -ER, add -É (accent distinguishes it from infinitive): manger → mangé, réserver → réservé, organiser → organisé. Avoir and aller share their irregular forms — in each pair, avoir is just aller minus the V: j'ai/je vais, tu as/tu vas, il a/il va. Pas encore = not yet (literally: not again — 'not this time yet').
sentences: J'ai déjà mangé, mais je n'ai pas encore payé.
I have already eaten, but I haven't paid yet.
Elle a organisé la fête. Tu as mangé ?
She has organised the party. Have you eaten?
Il a perdu les clés. Elle les a trouvées.
He has lost the keys. She has found them.
Nous avons cuisiné quelque chose. Ils l'ont mangé ?
We have cooked something. Have they eaten it?

build: Use avoir as the helper for these past-tense sentences.
For ER verbs, replace -er with -é.
Place pronouns before the helper when needed.
writing: Past participle -é is not the same spelling as -er.
J'ai contracts je + ai.
Déjà and pas encore need accents/spaces.
traps: Do not use the infinitive for the past participle.
Do not place pas around the participle; bracket the helper.

40.title: Passé Composé -u & Perdu
40.context: RE verbs in the past: remove -RE, add -U. Perdre → perdu. Past participle as adjective: je suis perdu = I am lost. The full verb system is now complete.
40.grammar: RE verb past participle: remove -RE, add -U: perdre → perdu, vendre → vendu, attendre → attendu. Fondue = melted (feminine past participle of fondre used as noun). Past participle as adjective after être: agrees in gender — je suis perdu (masc.), je suis perdue (fem.), elle est vendue (fem. noun). Exactly like English: 'I am lost' uses the past participle 'lost' as adjective after 'to be'.
words: lost (past part. of perdre as adj.)
sentences: Je suis totalement perdu. Tu l'as déjà vendu ?
I am totally lost. Have you already sold it?
Tu as encore perdu les clés ? Tu vas tout perdre.
Have you lost the keys again? You're going to lose everything.
Quand l'ont-ils perdu ? Nous avons déjà cherché partout.
When did they lose it? We have already looked everywhere.

build: For RE past participles, remove -re and add -u.
Use avoir for compound past in these practice sentences.
Use être + participle as an adjective for states like lost/sold.
writing: Perdu/vendu end in written u.
Adjectival participles can agree: perdue/vendue.
Quand l’ont-ils perdu has contraction and inversion.
traps: Do not use -é for RE past participles.
Do not ignore agreement when the participle is functioning as an adjective.
